claim: X-Ray supports cross-account observability, which lets you monitor and troubleshoot applications that span multiple accounts within an AWS Region and view cross-account traces in the X-Ray trace map and traces pages in the CloudWatch console.
q: Can X-Ray follow a request across several AWS accounts?
v: cross-account traces in the X-Ray trace map
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-crossaccount
AWS X-Ray supports *cross-account observability*, enabling you to monitor and troubleshoot applications that span multiple accounts within an AWS Region.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-crossaccount
You can view cross-account traces in the X-Ray trace map and traces pages within the [CloudWatch console](https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/).

claim: X-Ray supports tracing event-driven applications using Amazon SQS and AWS Lambda: traces from upstream message producers are automatically linked to traces from downstream Lambda consumer nodes, creating an end-to-end view of the application.
q: How can X-Ray trace a request that passes through an SQS queue to a Lambda consumer?
v: traces from downstream Lambda consumer nodes
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-tracelinking
AWS X-Ray supports tracing event-driven applications using Amazon SQS and AWS Lambda.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-tracelinking
Traces from upstream message producers are automatically linked to traces from downstream Lambda consumer nodes, creating an end-to-end view of the application.

claim: Transaction Search is an interactive analytics experience that gives complete visibility of your application transaction spans, the fundamental units of operation in a distributed trace.
q: What is X-Ray and CloudWatch Transaction Search?
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-transactionsearch

Transaction Search is an interactive analytics experience you can use to get complete visibility of your application transaction spans. Spans are the fundamental units of operation in a distributed trace and represent specific actions or tasks in an application or system.

claim: You can use OpenTelemetry to send traces directly to an OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) endpoint and get application performance monitoring experiences in CloudWatch Application Signals.
q: Can an application send OpenTelemetry traces directly to AWS without an agent?
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-opentelemetry

You can use OpenTelemetry to directly send traces to an OpenTelemetry Protocol (OTLP) endpoint, and get out-of-the box application performance monitoring experiences in [CloudWatch Application Signals](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/CloudWatch-Application-Monitoring-Intro.html).

claim: With the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) you can instrument your applications once and send correlated metrics and traces to multiple AWS monitoring solutions, including Amazon CloudWatch, AWS X-Ray and Amazon OpenSearch Service.
q: What does the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT) let you do?
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-instrumenting-your-app

With ADOT, engineers can instrument their applications once and send correlated metrics and traces to multiple AWS monitoring solutions including Amazon CloudWatch, AWS X-Ray, and Amazon OpenSearch Service.

claim: Using X-Ray with ADOT requires two components: an OpenTelemetry SDK enabled for use with X-Ray and the AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry Collector enabled for use with X-Ray.
q: Which two components does X-Ray with ADOT need?
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-instrumenting-your-app
Using X-Ray with ADOT requires two components: an *OpenTelemetry SDK* enabled for use with X-Ray, and the *AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry Collector* enabled for use with X-Ray.

claim: AWS services integrate with X-Ray at different levels: active instrumentation samples and instruments incoming requests, passive instrumentation instruments requests already sampled by another service, request tracing adds a tracing header to all incoming requests, and tooling runs the X-Ray daemon.
q: What do active and passive X-Ray instrumentation mean for an AWS service?
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services
*Active instrumentation* – Samples and instruments incoming requests
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services
*Passive instrumentation* – Instruments requests that have been sampled by another service
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services
*Request tracing* – Adds a tracing header to all incoming requests and propagates it downstream
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services
*Tooling* – Runs the X-Ray daemon to receive segments from the X-Ray SDK

claim: With X-Ray tracing enabled for a Lambda function, Lambda runs the X-Ray daemon and records a segment with details about invoking and running the function, and it traces requests that have already been sampled by another instrumented service without extra configuration.
q: What does Lambda do when X-Ray tracing is on for a function?
v: traces requests that have already been sampled
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-lambda
Lambda runs the [X-Ray daemon](xray-daemon.md) and records a segment with details about invoking and running the function.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-lambda
If your Lambda function is called by another instrumented service, Lambda traces requests that have already been sampled without any additional configuration.

claim: If a downstream Lambda function has traces enabled, the root Lambda function that calls it must also have traces enabled for the downstream function to generate traces.
q: Does a downstream Lambda function trace if the root function has tracing off?
v: traces enabled for the root Lambda function
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-lambda

If you have traces enabled for a downstream Lambda function, you must also have traces enabled for the root Lambda function that calls the downstream function in order for the downstream function to generate traces.

claim: Application Load Balancers add a trace ID to incoming HTTP requests in the X-Amzn-Trace-Id header, but load balancers do not send data to X-Ray and do not appear as a node on the service map.
q: Does an Application Load Balancer appear as a node on the X-Ray service map?
v: add a trace ID to incoming HTTP requests
do not send data to X-Ray
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-elb
Elastic Load Balancing application load balancers add a trace ID to incoming HTTP requests in a header named `X-Amzn-Trace-Id`.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-elb
Load balancers do not send data to X-Ray, and do not appear as a node on your service map.

claim: If a service traces requests with the X-Ray SDK, Amazon SQS can send the tracing header and continue to propagate the original trace from the sender to the consumer with a consistent trace ID; the AWSTraceHeader message system attribute overrides the HTTP trace header when both are set.
q: How does X-Ray keep one trace across an SQS queue?
v: from the sender to the consumer
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-sqs
If a service traces requests by using the X-Ray SDK, Amazon SQS can send the tracing header and continue to propagate the original trace from the sender to the consumer with a consistent trace ID.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-sqs
When both header instrumentations are set, the message system attribute overrides the HTTP trace header.

claim: Amazon SNS supports X-Ray tracing for both standard and FIFO topics; if you publish from a service already instrumented with X-Ray, SNS passes the trace context from publisher to subscribers.
q: Does Amazon SNS support X-Ray tracing for FIFO topics?
v: passes the trace context from publisher to subscribers
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-sns
Amazon SNS supports X-Ray tracing for both standard and FIFO topics.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-sns
If you publish to an Amazon SNS topic from a service that’s already instrumented with X-Ray, Amazon SNS passes the trace context from publisher to subscribers.

claim: AWS X-Ray integrates with AWS Step Functions to trace and analyze requests for Step Functions, so you can visualize the components of your state machine, identify performance bottlenecks and troubleshoot requests that resulted in an error.
q: What does X-Ray add for a Step Functions state machine?
v: trace and analyze requests for Step Functions
visualize the components of your state machine
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-services-stepfunctions

AWS X-Ray integrates with AWS Step Functions to trace and analyze requests for Step Functions. You can visualize the components of your state machine, identify performance bottlenecks, and troubleshoot requests that resulted in an error.

claim: AWS X-Ray always encrypts traces and related data at rest; when you need to audit and disable encryption keys for compliance, you can configure X-Ray to use an AWS KMS key.
q: Is X-Ray trace data encrypted at rest by default, and can you use your own key?
v: always encrypts traces and related data at rest
use an AWS Key Management Service
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-encryption

AWS X-Ray always encrypts traces and related data at rest. When you need to audit and disable encryption keys for compliance or internal requirements, you can configure X-Ray to use an AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key to encrypt data.

claim: X-Ray provides an AWS managed key named aws/xray for when you only want to audit key usage in CloudTrail; when you need to manage access to the key or configure key rotation you create a customer managed key.
q: When should you use a customer managed key instead of aws/xray for X-Ray?
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-encryption

X-Ray provides an AWS managed key named `aws/xray`. Use this key when you just want to [audit key usage in AWS CloudTrail](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/logging-using-cloudtrail.html) and don't need to manage the key itself. When you need to manage access to the key or configure key rotation, you can [create a customer managed key](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/create-keys.html).

claim: When you change X-Ray encryption settings, existing data is not re-encrypted, and while the new key is being processed X-Ray may encrypt data with a combination of the new and old settings.
q: Is old trace data re-encrypted when you switch the X-Ray encryption key?
v: a combination of the new and old settings
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-encryption
While the new key is being processed, X-Ray may encrypt data with a combination of the new and old settings. Existing data is not re-encrypted when you change encryption settings.

claim: AWS KMS charges when X-Ray uses a KMS key to encrypt or decrypt trace data.
v: AWS KMS charges when X-Ray uses a KMS key
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-console-encryption
AWS KMS charges when X-Ray uses a KMS key to encrypt or decrypt trace data.

claim: X-Ray data events such as PutTraceSegments can be logged to CloudTrail, but by default CloudTrail does not log data events, the Event history does not record them, and additional charges apply.
q: Are X-Ray PutTraceSegments calls logged by CloudTrail by default?
v: By default, CloudTrail doesn’t log data events
ev: docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-api-cloudtrail
Data events provide information about the resource operations performed on or in a resource (for example, PutTraceSegments, which uploads segment documents to X-Ray).
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-api-cloudtrail

These are also known as data plane operations. Data events are often high-volume activities. By default, CloudTrail doesn’t log data events. The CloudTrail **Event history** doesn't record data events.
docs/xray/latest/devguide/xray-api-cloudtrail
Additional charges apply for data events.
